science.title: DNA methylation modulation by 5-Azacytidine regulates EMT markers and reduces invasiveness in docetaxel-resistant prostate cancer cells
science.description: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) is associated with poor prognosis and high mortality, largely due to androgen and chemotherapy resistance. This study investigated whether global DNA hypomethylation induced through DNMT1 inhibition could reduce invasion and motility in docetaxel-resistant (DR) prostate cancer (PCa). Parental and DR PCa cell lines (22Rv1, PC3, and DU145) were treated with 5-Azacytidine (5-AZA), which reduced cell viability in a dose-dependent manner in all models except DU145-DR cells. DNMT1 inhibition was achieved in all cell lines and was associated with significant reductions in invasion in DU145-DR (p < 0.05) and PC3-DR (p < 0.01) cells, together with reduced migration in both resistant models. Transcript-level analysis showed cell line-dependent modulation of EMT-associated markers following 5-AZA treatment. In DU145-DR cells, CDH1 was upregulated, TJP1 increased, VIM decreased, and SNAI2 remained unchanged. In PC3-DR cells, CDH1 remained largely unchanged, TJP1 was downregulated, and no significant changes were observed in SNAI2 or VIM. Protein analyses showed similar cell line-dependent effects: DU145-DR cells displayed a slight increase in ZO-1 with no evident changes in E-cadherin or vimentin, whereas PC3-DR cells showed increased E-cadherin and ZO-1 with unchanged vimentin. Overall, 5-AZA attenuated EMT-associated traits in resistant cells.

science.title: How plants selectively silence jumping genes while protecting essential ones
science.description: Histone variants help establish DNA methylation at transposons (jumping genes) while preventing this epigenetic modification from spreading to essential genes in plants, a study from the Institute of Science Tokyo reveals. By revealing how these chromosome-associated proteins guide the formation of precise epigenomic patterns, the findings provide new insights into the selective silencing of transposons, laying the groundwork for future epigenome-editing technologies for crop improvement and disease research.
